name: Tasman Peninsula
tagline: Convict ruins and Australia's highest sea cliffs, an easy run from Hobart.
description: The Tasman Peninsula hangs off Tasmania's south-east, joined to the mainland by the narrow isthmus at Eaglehawk Neck. It was the centre of convict transportation, and the Port Arthur penitentiary and the Coal Mines are World Heritage-listed parts of the Australian Convict Sites. The coast is just as big a draw, with dolerite capes, sea arches, caves and blowholes cut into the cliffs of Tasman National Park. Most visitors base in Port Arthur, Nubeena or Eaglehawk Neck and fit it around a Hobart stay.

goodToKnow.title: Parks pass and Three Capes booking
goodToKnow.detail: Tasman National Park needs a valid Tasmanian parks pass, and the Three Capes Track is booked ahead because passes are limited.

goodToKnow.title: Blowhole Road is unsealed
goodToKnow.detail: The coast road to Tasman Arch, Devils Kitchen and the Blowhole is unsealed with limited parking, so go early in peak season.

goodToKnow.title: Weather on the cliffs
goodToKnow.detail: Cape tracks are exposed to wind and sudden weather off the Southern Ocean, so carry layers and keep well back from unfenced cliff edges.

name: Freycinet
tagline: Pink granite peaks around Tasmania's best-known crescent beach.
description: Freycinet National Park covers the Freycinet Peninsula on the east coast, with the pink granite Hazards range rising behind sheltered turquoise bays. It was founded in 1916, making it one of Tasmania's two oldest parks. Wineglass Bay is the headline view, but the park also has quieter beaches, lighthouse cliffs and granite summits. Most visitors stay in Coles Bay or Swansea and drive in for the day.
whyVisit: Walk down to Wineglass Bay's beach
whyVisitSubjects: Wineglass Bay seen from the lookout
Wineglass Bay white sand beach
Mount Amos summit with the view over Wineglass Bay
Cape Tourville Lighthouse and its coastal boardwalk

goodToKnow.title: Parks pass required
goodToKnow.detail: A valid Tasmanian parks pass is needed to enter, and a day pass for a vehicle covers its occupants.

goodToKnow.title: Tracks are steep and rocky
goodToKnow.detail: Walks run over steep granite and loose gravel, so wear sturdy shoes and carry water, especially on Mount Amos and the Wineglass Bay beach walk.

goodToKnow.title: Drive carefully at dusk
goodToKnow.detail: Wallabies and wombats are on the roads from dusk to dawn, and an advisory 60 km/h limit applies near the park after dark.

name: Bicheno
tagline: A small east-coast fishing town with a blowhole, wildlife and penguins at dusk.
description: Bicheno is a small coastal town on the Tasman Highway, known for its colony of little penguins and as a base for Freycinet National Park. A waterfront track links the Gulch harbour, the blowhole and Diamond Island. Inland, Douglas-Apsley National Park has dry forest, gorges and swimming waterholes. Penguin tours run at night, and numbers are highest in summer.

goodToKnow.title: Book penguin tours ahead
goodToKnow.detail: Penguin tours run nightly and are capped at 120 people, so book ahead in summer; there are almost none ashore in winter.

goodToKnow.title: The blowhole is unfenced
goodToKnow.detail: Waves can crash right over it in big seas, so stay well back from the edge, especially in storms and high tides.

goodToKnow.title: Penguins on the road
goodToKnow.detail: Take care driving at night, particularly on the Tasman Highway near the Diamond Island end of town.

name: Launceston
tagline: Tasmania's second city, with a wild gorge a short walk from the centre.
description: Launceston was settled in 1805 and is Tasmania's second-largest city, about 87,000 people at the 2021 census. It is the main base for northern Tasmania, with Victorian streets, a museum and art gallery, and a historic brewery. Cataract Gorge, 1 km from the centre, has trails, a swimming pool and a chairlift across the South Esk River. Convict-era estates at Longford and the Tamar Valley are short drives away.

whyVisitSubjects: Cataract Gorge and its suspension bridge

goodToKnow.title: Gorge parking is paid
goodToKnow.detail: Parking at the gorge entrance is paid, by the hour or all day, but walking in and swimming are free.

goodToKnow.title: A car helps
goodToKnow.detail: A car is the easiest way around, and the Longford estates, the Tamar Valley and Freycinet are all driving distance; the city also has a Metro bus service.

goodToKnow.title: Swim with care
goodToKnow.detail: The gorge water is cold with a current, so use the constructed entrances or the free, unheated pool.

name: Tamar Valley
tagline: Cool-climate wines, wildlife and river lighthouses along the Tamar.
description: The Tamar Valley runs north from Launceston along the Tamar River to Bass Strait, and is Tasmania's largest wine region, with more than 20 vineyards on the Tamar Valley Wine Route. Pinot noir and chardonnay are the main grapes. Along the river, Beauty Point has a platypus house and a seahorse farm, and Low Head Lighthouse marks the river mouth. Beaconsfield's former gold mine is known for the 2006 rescue of two trapped miners.

goodToKnow.title: Pick a driver
goodToKnow.detail: Cellar doors are spread along both banks, so allow a day, choose a designated driver and follow the wine route signs.

goodToKnow.title: Drive from Launceston
goodToKnow.detail: The valley is a drive of about 30 to 60 minutes from Launceston, and a car is the practical way to link the towns and lookouts.

goodToKnow.title: Book wildlife visits
goodToKnow.detail: Platypus House runs guided visits, so check times before driving to Beauty Point.

name: Bay of Fires
tagline: White beaches and orange lichen-covered granite on the north-east coast.
description: The Bay of Fires is a run of white beaches, clear blue water and orange granite boulders on Tasmania's north-east coast, stretching from Binalong Bay to Eddystone Point. The orange colour comes from lichen. Captain Tobias Furneaux named it in 1773 after the fires he saw Aboriginal people lighting on the beaches. The northern end lies in Mount William National Park, while the southern end is a conservation area, with St Helens the main base.

goodToKnow.title: Parks pass in Mount William
goodToKnow.detail: The northern end sits in Mount William National Park, which needs a valid Tasmanian parks pass.

goodToKnow.title: Base in St Helens
goodToKnow.detail: St Helens is the largest town on the coast, about two hours from Launceston, with the nearest services and Bay of Fires access.

goodToKnow.title: The sea is cold
goodToKnow.detail: Water stays cold even in summer, and the beaches are open with little shelter, so bring a windproof layer.

name: Stanley
tagline: A historic fishing village beneath a flat-topped volcanic plug on Bass Strait.
description: Stanley is a village of about 550 people in the north-west, best known for The Nut, a volcanic plug rising 143 m beside the sea and visible from almost everywhere in town. A chairlift and a steep zigzag track climb it, and a circuit on top looks over Bass Strait and Rocky Cape National Park. The town has colonial buildings, and Highfield, a Regency-style homestead nearby, is open to visitors. Little penguins come ashore here after dark.
whyVisitSubjects: The Nut volcanic plug above Stanley

goodToKnow.title: Car access only
goodToKnow.detail: The only way into Stanley is by car; it is a little over an hour from Burnie, so plan the drive in.

goodToKnow.title: Chairlift or zigzag track
goodToKnow.detail: Ride the chairlift up The Nut, or take the steeper Zig Zag Track, then walk the 4.6 km circuit on top (about an hour).

goodToKnow.title: Penguin etiquette
goodToKnow.detail: At the viewing area just after dark, do not use flash or a bright torch, which can harm the penguins' eyes; a red light is better.
